strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important question in masked diffusion models: inference-time unmasking order selection, going beyond ad hoc heuristics like max-confidence/margin.

The KL-regularized MDP formulation with an explicit reference policy is clean, and the paper provides policy-improvement and KL-tightening guarantees (Theorem 2 is adapted to the MDM setting), plus three tractable surrogate objectives with derivations in the appendix.
The memory-efficient design (frozen 8B MDM + 134M trainable policy, feature reuse, token-wise gradient updates, single A100 training) is practical and well-documented with full training algorithms.

Empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: four benchmarks (SUDOKU, ZEBRA, GSM8K, MATH500), four heuristic baselines, ablations over reference-policy realizations (gconf, softmax, Top-K), regularization ablations, and a compatibility study showing gains on top of diffu-GRPO post-training.
The Pass@N motivating experiment (Figure 1) convincingly demonstrates that better unmasking paths exist beyond max-confidence, motivating a learned scheduler.
The SUDOKU gain (+11.2% over max-confidence, 70.5% to 81.7%) is substantial in the setting where unmasking order matters most.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core contribution: applying GRPO with a reference policy to train an unmasking policy is an incremental combination of existing tools (GRPO/DeepSeek-R1 style objective, Mroueh 2025's analysis), and is closely related to DCOLT (Huang et al., 2025), which already trains an unmasking policy via RL; the comparison to DCOLT is indirect (via a 'randomly initialized' ablation claimed to be 'conceptually equivalent') rather than a direct head-to-head under matched setups.

Theoretical results are weaker than the abstract suggests: Theorem 1 is explicitly a restatement of Mroueh (2025); Theorem 2 relies on idealized assumptions (an MDM with L_MDM=0, terminal 0/1 reward, support conditions) that do not hold in practice — notably, the actual experiments use fractional rewards for SUDOKU, contradicting the binary reward assumption of the theory. The gap between stated guarantees and practice is not clearly acknowledged.

Empirical margins are modest on most benchmarks: +1.9% on ZEBRA over entropy, +1.9% on GSM8K over confidence, and a tie with margin on MATH500; no statistical significance tests, error bars, or multiple seeds are reported, so small gains are hard to interpret.

Evaluation is limited to a single base model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct); generalization of the learned policy is unclear — policies appear to be trained per-benchmark, and cross-domain transfer or text-generation quality metrics (e.g., likelihood/perplexity) beyond verifiable tasks are absent.

Several technical choices are heuristic despite the 'principled' framing: the Top-K realization restricts the action space to K positions, the cross-entropy divergence for gconf is admitted to be 'not theoretical', and Eq. (29) contains a notation error (gθ vs. gϕ); the justification of the KL surrogate (Propositions 2-3) provides upper bounds but no tightness analysis.

The relationship between reward maximization (task accuracy) and the claimed objective of 'matching the data distribution' is loose; improving verifiable-task accuracy does not directly establish that samples are closer to p_data, and the KL-tightening result addresses the ideal-MDM case only.

Some important details for reproducibility (hyperparameters, training data sizes, number of RL steps, β values, sampling cost during training) are deferred or incomplete, and the computational overhead of RL rollouts relative to the memory-efficiency claims is not quantified.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: learning the unmasking order in MDMs instead of relying on ad hoc heuristics like max-confidence, with an empirical motivation (Pass@N analysis in Fig. 1) showing better unmasking paths exist

Formulating unmasking as a KL-regularized MDP with an explicit reference policy and deriving policy-improvement / KL-tightening guarantees is a coherent framing, and the writing makes the gap between the intractable ideal objective and the practical surrogate loss transparent

Practical design is appealing: training only a small (134M) policy model on top of a frozen 8B MDM with a memory-efficient token-by-token gradient procedure (single A100 40GB), which is complementary to methods like diffu-GRPO (Table 3 shows +1.3% on top of post-trained MDM)

Consistent empirical improvements over random, margin, entropy, and confidence schedulers across four benchmarks, plus ablations on the choice of reference policy (max-confidence vs. softmax vs. Top-K realizations) and on the effect of the KL/CE regularizer
Honest reporting that max-confidence remains a strong single-path baseline, and the paper ties (Math500) rather than always wins
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 1 is explicitly a restatement of the GRPO convergence result of Mroueh (2025), Theorem 2 is a fairly direct corollary applied to MDMs, and Propositions 1-3 are standard policy-gradient / REINFORCE derivations specialized to this setting; the core mathematical machinery is largely imported rather than new

Closest prior work (DCOLT, Huang et al. 2025) also trains an unmasking policy via RL, but is only discussed conceptually and never compared with empirically; without this comparison it is hard to attribute gains to the KL-regularized reference-policy framework rather than to RL fine-tuning of the scheduler in general

Evaluation scope is narrow and weak on standard language tasks: four benchmarks dominated by logic puzzles (SUDOKU, Zebra) and small gains elsewhere; MATH500 ties the best baseline (28.4%) and GSM8K gains are modest; no perplexity/likelihood or open-ended generation evaluation, no error bars, seeds, or significance testing for the reported deltas

The theory-practice gap is acknowledged but unresolved: the max-confidence realization replaces the KL term with a cross-entropy surrogate that is admitted to be 'not theoretical', and the guarantees require an 'ideal MDM' with zero MDM loss plus support assumptions that plainly do not hold for LLaDA-8B

The motivating Fig. 1 comparison is somewhat unfair: Top-5 Pass@N with N=10 samples naturally exceeds a deterministic single-path baseline, so 'better paths exist' does not by itself justify the learned-policy machinery

The learned policy appears to be trained and evaluated per-benchmark (trained on GSM8K/SUDOKU, then evaluated per task) with unclear cross-task generalization; the practical value of a separate 134M policy model per task versus simply tuning existing heuristics is not established

Several claims rest on conjecture rather than evidence (e.g., why Top-K helps on GSM8K vs. max-confidence on SUDOKU is explained only post hoc as 'conjecture'), and the best configuration differs per task, which weakens the generality of the method

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: the choice of unmasking order is a known bottleneck for masked diffusion models (MDMs), and learning the scheduler is a natural next step beyond heuristics like max-confidence/max-margin.

Clean problem formulation: casting unmasking position selection as a KL-regularized MDP over a frozen MDM, with verifiable terminal rewards, is well-motivated and clearly presented; the RL environment dynamics (agent chooses where to unmask, environment induced by πθ) are precisely specified.

Includes theoretical analysis with policy-improvement (Theorem 1) and KL-tightening (Theorem 2) guarantees, plus rigorous derivations of tractable surrogates (Propositions 1–3, Lemma 2) tailored to the sparse-reward, non-stationary, finite-horizon setting.

Practically appealing architecture: a small (134M) policy model on top of a frozen 8B MDM enables memory-efficient training on a single A100, which is a real engineering contribution for large-scale MDMs.

Solid empirical coverage: four benchmarks (SUDOKU, ZEBRA, GSM8K, MATH500), four heuristic baselines (random, margin, entropy, confidence), ablations over reference-policy realizations (max-confidence, softmax, Top-K) and over the divergence term, plus a demonstrated compatibility with diffu-GRPO showing complementary gains.

Consistent empirical trend: the learned policy matches or outperforms all heuristics on every benchmark, with a substantial 11.2% gain over max-confidence on SUDOKU where unmasking order matters most.
Honest positioning relative to closely related concurrent work (DCOLT, diffu-GRPO), with the distinction (KL-regularized MDP with reference policy for a frozen MDM) clearly articulated.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 1 is explicitly a restatement of Mroueh (2025); Theorem 2 is a relatively straightforward KL comparison under strong idealized assumptions (existence of an ideal MDM with zero loss, full support of the reference policy, r=1 on the entire support). The core theoretical machinery is imported rather than developed.

Gap between theory and practice: the guarantees apply to the unclipped output-level objective (Eq. 10), but training uses a clipped token-level surrogate with CE or a bespoke LKL estimator for the max-confidence reference where the KL is ill-posed. The paper acknowledges this ('Although not theoretical...'), which weakens the central claim that the guarantees justify the method.

Empirical gains are mixed in magnitude: beyond SUDOKU, improvements are modest (Zebra: 36.2 vs 35.1 for entropy; MATH500 ties max-margin at 28.4; GSM8K +1.9%). No confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance testing are reported, so the 'consistently outperforms' claim is under-supported for the smaller margins.

Missing head-to-head comparison with the closest prior work (DCOLT, Huang et al. 2025): the ablation with a randomly initialized policy is claimed to be 'conceptually equivalent' to DCOLT, but this is not identical and no direct empirical comparison is provided.

Evaluation is limited to a single base MDM (LLaDA-8B-Instruct); generalization to other MDMs (e.g., Dream-7B) or non-verifiable/open-ended generation tasks is untested, limiting the scope of the conclusions.

The Pass@N analysis in Section 3.1 is weak evidence for 'existence of an optimal path beyond max-confidence': Pass@N naturally increases with N for any stochastic scheduler, so surpassing the deterministic single-path line does not by itself establish that a learnable better ordering exists.

The distribution-matching motivation (closer to pdata) is somewhat in tension with the reward-maximization objective and the partial-credit reward on SUDOKU; the KL-tightening result does not directly certify the empirically measured accuracy gains.

Reproducibility gaps in the main text: key hyperparameters (β, clip ε, group size G, learning rates, training data sizes, number of training prompts) are not specified on the main pages, and there are typos that could confuse (e.g., 'Let let gref', Eq. 29 writes log gθ(a|xn) where gϕ is meant, Eq. 85's log p_gref(x_{1:L}|x0) term, missing 'be' in 'can interpreted').

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: learning the unmasking order for masked diffusion models instead of relying on ad hoc heuristics such as max-confidence is a relevant and timely question, supported by an informative motivating experiment (Pass@N analysis in Section 3.1) showing that better unmasking trajectories exist.

Solid theoretical framing: casting unmasking as a KL-regularized MDP, with policy-improvement (Theorem 1) and KL-tightening (Theorem 2) guarantees, plus careful derivation of tractable surrogate losses (Propositions 1–3, trajectory-level KL upper bound, gradient alignment). Proofs in Appendix C are detailed and reasonably rigorous for this setting.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four benchmarks (SUDOKU, ZEBRA, GSM8K, MATH500) on a strong base model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct), comparisons against four heuristic samplers (random, margin, entropy, confidence), ablations over reference-policy realizations, binary vs. dense reward, and complementarity with diffu-GRPO post-training (Table 3).

Practical, memory-efficient training recipe (Algorithm 2) with a small policy model (134M vs 8B), single-A100 training, and released code; useful qualitative visualizations (Figures 9–10) illustrating failure modes of max-confidence.

Honest discussion of limitations: authors explicitly report smaller gains on GSM8K/MATH500, conjecture causes, and include a preliminary generalization study with an ARM-likelihood reward (Appendix D.2).
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 1 is an explicit restatement of Mroueh (2025), and Theorem 2 is a direct application of that result to the MDM setting; the contribution of the theory is mostly adaptation rather than new analysis.

Incremental novelty over concurrent/prior work: relative to DCOLT (Huang et al., 2025), the main differences are the KL-regularized objective with an explicit reference policy, and the measured gains over the DCOLT-equivalent ablation are only ~2–3% on the two benchmarks where it is compared.

Gains are inconsistent and modest on the main language benchmarks: on MATH500 the method only ties the margin baseline (0.284 vs 0.284) rather than beating it, and on GSM8K the improvement over max-confidence is 1.9%; the strongest configuration differs per task (max-confidence realization for SUDOKU/ZEBRA, Top-K for GSM8K/MATH500), which effectively means task-specific hyperparameter selection without a principled way to choose it a priori.

Potential evaluation inflation: models are saved every 100 steps and the best accuracy is reported (following diffu-GRPO), which constitutes checkpoint selection on the test set; no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance testing are provided for the headline comparisons.

The theoretical guarantees rely on a binary terminal reward, but the main experiments use a dense reward (fraction of correct slots; plus an auxiliary log-probability term for GSM8K/MATH500), so the empirical setup is not fully aligned with the theory; the max-confidence realization further replaces the KL term with an admittedly 'not theoretical' cross-entropy surrogate.
Additional inference cost of running the policy model alongside the MDM at every denoising step is not quantified, which matters when comparing against zero-cost heuristics.

Generality remains unproven: all policies are trained per benchmark with task-specific rewards; the generalization study (Appendix D.2) is preliminary and does not demonstrate a single policy transferring across tasks.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely question in masked diffusion models: replacing heuristic unmasking schedules (max-confidence, max-margin, entropy) with a learned position-selection policy.
The KL-regularized MDP framing with a heuristic reference policy is sensible, and the paper is transparent that Theorem 1 is a restatement of prior work (Mroueh, 2025).

Practical system contributions are decent: the lightweight policy architecture (frozen 8B MDM + 134M policy), memory-efficient two-phase training algorithm, and release of code support reproducibility.
The motivating Pass@N experiment (Section 3.1) is a nice, simple piece of evidence that higher-yield unmasking trajectories exist beyond max-confidence.
Clear ablations: reference-policy realizations, regularization effect on group reward variance, compatibility with diffu-GRPO post-training, and binary vs. dense reward settings.
Qualitative Sudoku trajectory visualizations (Appendix F) effectively illustrate the failure modes of max-confidence that the learned policy avoids.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over the closest prior work: DCOLT (Huang et al., 2025) already trains the unmasking policy via RL; the main delta is adding a KL-regularizer with an explicit reference policy. Theorem 1 is explicitly a restatement of Mroueh (2025), and Theorem 2 is a fairly direct corollary of Mroueh's Lemma 1 with a KL expansion. The theoretical contribution is thin and rests on idealized assumptions (zero-loss ideal MDM, exact GRPO fixed-point convergence) that are far from the practical setting.

Empirical gains are inconsistent and small on the benchmarks where unmasking order supposedly matters least/most: MATH500 only ties the margin baseline (0.284 vs. 0.284), and GSM8K improves max-confidence by only ~1.9 points, whereas the headline 11.2% gain is specific to 4x4 Sudoku—a toy setting with a tiny action/vocabulary space.

Evaluation methodology has a validity concern: models are saved every 100 steps and the best evaluation accuracy is reported, which amounts to model selection on the test set and can inflate reported gains, especially for the small improvements on GSM8K/MATH500.

Task-specificity is under-addressed: a separate policy is trained per benchmark (with SFT for Zebra), and there is no experiment showing the learned policy generalizes across tasks or that a single policy can serve multiple domains, which limits the practical significance of replacing a training-free heuristic.

The theoretically aligned binary verifiable reward (the setting the theorems actually cover) is relegated to the appendix; main results use a dense reward augmented with the MDM's own log-probabilities, which decouples the headline experiments from the theoretical guarantees.

Only one base MDM (LLaDA-8B-Instruct) is evaluated; no results on Dream-7B or other MDMs, no seed variance or significance testing for the small deltas, and no comparison of inference-time overhead of the policy versus the heuristics.

The relation to data-distribution matching (Theorem 2) is largely rhetorical for practical use: the empirical results measure task accuracy, not any direct KL improvement to p_data, so the claimed 'provably closer to the data distribution' framing overstates what the experiments support.

Several design choices feel ad hoc despite the regularization framing (e.g., cross-entropy regularization for the deterministic g_conf because the KL is ill-posed, rank-based relative log-prob rewards), weakening the claim of a principled framework.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: replacing heuristic unmasking schedules (max-confidence/max-margin) with a learned scheduler addresses a real, recognized limitation of MDM inference, and the Pass@N analysis in Section 3.1 convincingly establishes that better unmasking trajectories exist than max-confidence.

Coherent technical framework: casting unmasking as a KL-regularized MDP with a strong heuristic reference policy, deriving tractable token-level surrogates (Propositions 1-3), and providing multiple practical realizations (max-confidence, softmax, Top-K) is a well-executed design.

Consistent empirical gains across four benchmarks (SUDOKU, ZEBRA, GSM8K, MATH500) with a strong baseline suite (random, margin, entropy, confidence), plus ablations on the divergence term and binary vs. dense reward; evaluation under the theoretically aligned binary reward setting (Table 4) is good practice.

Practically valuable engineering: memory-efficient training on top of a frozen 8B MDM with a 134M policy model (single A100 40GB), and demonstrated complementarity with diffu-GRPO (+1.3% over max-confidence on post-trained LLaDA), showing the method stacks with MDM post-training.
Code is released and the appendix is thorough (algorithms, full derivations, hyperparameters, prompt templates, qualitative unmasking visualizations), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Theoretical novelty is limited: Theorem 1 is an explicit restatement of Mroueh (2025), and Theorem 2 is a fairly direct extension using the restated policy dynamics. The assumptions are strong and not verified in practice (existence of an ideal MDM with zero loss, local fixed-point condition |h'|<1, support conditions), so the gap between theory and the deployed objective is substantial.

The practical objective deviates from the theory in central ways: the main experiments use a dense reward (fraction of correct slots plus log-probability auxiliary) rather than the binary verifiable reward that the theory covers, and for the max-confidence realization the divergence term is replaced by an admittedly 'not theoretical' cross-entropy (Appendix B.1). This weakens the claim that the guarantees explain the empirical success.

Gains on the general reasoning benchmarks are modest and possibly within noise: MATH500 ties the margin baseline (0.284 vs 0.284) and GSM8K improves by ~2% over max-confidence; no seeds/error bars or statistical significance tests are reported.

Per-task training and evaluation protocol raise concerns: the policy is trained separately per benchmark with task-specific rewards, and following diffu-GRPO the authors 'save models every 100 steps and report the best accuracy,' which is a form of test-set selection; generalization to other tasks is only a preliminary study in Appendix D.2 (reward-driven log-likelihood improvement, not head-to-head comparisons).

Baseline comparison with the closest prior work (DCOLT, Huang et al. 2025) is indirect: the 'random initialization' ablation is claimed to be 'conceptually equivalent to DCOLT' rather than an actual comparison under DCOLT's own training setup.

Only one base MDM (LLaDA-8B-Instruct) and relatively small synthetic datasets (4x4 SUDOKU) are used; the auxiliary reward based on the MDM's own log-probabilities partly conflates the learned ordering policy with the MDM's existing confidence signal, making it hard to isolate the contribution of learned ordering heuristics.
